programme.title: Young, British and Tradwife
programme.desc:
Tradwives are trending. The term is in the dictionary, and the hashtag has over 300 million views on TikTok. Online tradwives promote the pleasures of domesticity and teach others how to be perfect homemakers in effortless and elegant social media videos that generate millions of likes. But they are not just an online phenomenon. Women in the real world, inspired by online influencers, are increasingly rejecting feminism, workplace hustle and hook-up culture to bake sourdough, homeschool the kids and obey their husbands.
BAFTA- and Grierson Award-nominated documentarian Poppy Jay wants to know why the tradwife world of domestic chores and submission appeals to so many. Reflecting on her own experience of forced marriage, she packs away her camera, pins on an apron and meets with British tradwives to find out if this is what true choice looks like in the 21st century.
As she juggles baking, sewing and schooling, she asks if a movement that demands submission to a husband is the solution to modern burnout or just the latest manifestation of an age-old misogynistic culture shaped by men, for men.
Poppy meets women from across the tradwife spectrum, from the newly married coach of ‘biblical wifery’ with 70,000 TikTok followers to the homeschooling mother of seven, to discover why the simple life rooted in traditional Christian values is suddenly so popular. Immersing herself in family life, Poppy challenges her own preconceptions, asking why any women would choose to submit to her husband and whether feminism has, as the tradwives claim, betrayed women by promising them they can have it all. They’ll need to be fixed before luthier Julyan can even think about starting the cosmetic work required to the veneer.

He’s at Dave Smith’s workshop, overlooking the harbour, to try his hand at the lost art of brilliant cutting before turning a newly decorated piece of glass into a Victorian-style mirror. As Dave can boast clients like David Beckham, John Meyer and Disney, it’s a rare chance for Dom to get some tips straight from a master craftsman. Fish and chips by the sea are an added bonus. programme.title: The Repair Shop on the Road
programme.sub-title: Ayrshire - Restoring Robert Burns Graffiti ║ S1
programme.desc:
Carpenter Will and horologist Steve are far from home today, exploring Ayrshire on Scotland’s west coast. Their first stop is the Scottish Boat Building School in Irvine, where Tom is waiting with a very unusual vessel. It’s a three-piece canoe designed in the 1930s and small enough to fit in the guard’s van of a train, which meant tourists could bring their own canoes on holiday in the years before owning a car was commonplace. It represents a different kind of freedom for Tom, though. His achondroplasia means a regular-size canoe is too difficult to manoeuvre. If this folding version can be fixed, he will finally have the freedom to take his daughter out exploring the waterways of Britain.
Ayrshire is the birthplace of Scotland’s national poet, Robert Burns, and many of the towns and villages in the region can boast strong links to his life and works. So it’s no surprise that when Will is called to Barr Castle in Galston, he comes face-to-face with a very special artefact. It’s a windowpane with a hand inscription by Robert Burns himself. However, it has suffered some damage in the past, so for decades its current custodians have had it hidden away in a cupboard for safekeeping. With the help of ceramics expert Kirsten Ramsay, they hope to once again put it on display. Fixing glass is notoriously difficult, and Kirsten definitely feels the pressure of getting such an important object looking back to its best.
While in the area, Steve takes the chance to visit Kays in Mauchline, who have been crafting curling stones for over 170 years. Using a dense granite quarried from a single Scottish island, these dedicated craftspeople hone stones of unparalleled quality for use in the Winter Olympics. Steve gets the chance to help with the process, but will it be gold, silver or bronze for his efforts? Marcus and Monica are joined by special guest Adejoké Bakare, whose restaurant Chishuru is at the forefront of West African fine dining. Now she’s setting the chefs a dish from her own repertoire: mushroom moin moin, served with a shito sauce and steamed egg.

With no recipe to follow, they’ll have to rely entirely on their palates, instincts and technical skills to recreate Adejoké’s dish. programme.title: BBC New Comedy Awards
programme.desc:
The BBC’s biggest comedy talent search has reached its final night. Almost 1,000 comedians applied to this year’s New Comedy Awards. More than 100 went head-to-head at showcases across the country, and just 30 made it through to the knockout heats. Now only six remain.
The finalists take to the stage one last time, each hoping to win over the judges and be crowned BBC New Comedian 2026.
The grand final is filmed in front of a full house at Birmingham’s iconic Town Hall. Presenting the night is award-winning writer, comedian and Hollywood actor Guz Khan, who made the journey from stand-up to the screen and knows exactly what the night means to the acts waiting in the wings.
Leading the judging panel is the multitalented and multi-award-winning comedian, actor and writer Amy Gledhill. Joining her are Kiell Smith-Bynoe, star of Ghosts and Taskmaster, and Dan Tiernan, a former BBC New Comedy Awards winner. Together, they weigh up the writing, the delivery and the originality of every act before choosing their winner.
Rounding off the night is a very special performance from last year’s winner, Eli Hart, who returns to hand over the award to this year’s champion.
The winner will receive a paid commission to write and perform their own 30-minute audio pilot under the mentorship of a BBC comedy commissioner, plus a trophy and £1,000 in cash. For a comic at the start of their career, it is a rare opportunity that could open plenty of doors.
Now in their 30th year, the New Comedy Awards have helped launch the careers of comedy greats who regularly feature on our stages and screens, including Peter Kay, Lee Mack, Russell Howard, Romesh Ranganathan, Alan Carr, Sarah Millican, Josie Long and Joe Lycett.
The finalists are hoping to follow in their footsteps.
Six comics. One stage. One title. Who will be crowned BBC New Comedian 2026? programme.title: MasterChef: The Professionals
programme.desc:
It’s quarter-final time again as the standout chefs from this week’s heats come together for another battle in the kitchen. The stakes are higher, the challenges more demanding, and the judges’ expectations are greater than ever.
First up is the invention test, where the chefs must make a surprise ingredient the star of the show. This time, it’s saffron, one of the world’s most-prized spices, renowned for its distinctive aroma, delicate floral notes and rich golden hue. But its extraordinary character comes with a challenge. Too little and its subtle flavour can disappear, but too much or poorly handled and it can overwhelm a dish with bitterness. The chefs must find the perfect balance, using their creativity and instinct to showcase saffron at its best. With just 70 minutes to cook and serve, can they transform this precious ingredient into something truly exceptional?
Next, the chefs face one of their toughest tests yet, cooking a two-course menu for three of the country’s leading food writers and critics, Leyla Kazim, Xanthe Clay and David Ellis. These seasoned critics know what separates a competent chef from a potential star, and this is a chance for the competitors to demonstrate the depth of their talent, with dishes that combine outstanding flavour, technical skill and individuality.
Taking the critics’ feedback into account, Marcus and Monica must now decide who has done enough to secure a place in knockout week. With the competition entering its most demanding phase, only the chefs who consistently deliver at the highest level will remain in the race for the coveted crown. programme.title: Songs of Praise
programme.desc:
International Men’s Day was established in 1999 to highlight positive male role models and raise awareness of men’s health and wellbeing. Ahead of this year’s event, Sean Fletcher is in Leeds exploring what it means to be a man in modern society, and how faith, friendship and a sense of purpose can help men thrive in mind, body and spirit.
He meets rugby league legend Jamie Jones-Buchanan, now CEO of Leeds Rhinos, where he made 421 appearances, as well as representing England and Great Britain. Jamie reflects on growing up without a father figure in one of the UK’s most deprived areas, and how rugby and his Christian faith provided positive male role models, and a sense of belonging and purpose. He challenges stereotypes of the macho rugby player, and his passion for helping the next generation comes to life during a training session.
In the Welsh valleys, Pastor John Funnell reflects on the extraordinary number of young men joining his congregation. John left a highly paid career after becoming a Christian and moved to one of Europe’s most deprived communities. He explains how his church offers practical skills, mentoring, friendship and faith, helping men see that their past does not have to determine their future.
Back in Leeds, Sean meets Chris Sayburn, a minister and renowned worship leader who spent 12 years living with chronic pain following complications after spinal surgery. He tells Sean how exercise and faith have helped him rebuild his life and how a community of men became a lifeline.
With uplifting hymns and songs from around the UK.

programme.title: Blue Planet III
programme.desc:
The open ocean is the largest wilderness on earth. Covering more than half of the planet's surface, it appears at first glance to be an endless blue desert. Yet hidden here are some of the most extraordinary animals.
We uncover the surprising strategies, epic journeys and remarkable resilience that allows life to thrive here. From wandering predators and drifting castaways to giant whales and tiny turtle hatchlings, it is a world where life survives against the odds.
The journey begins far beyond the sight of land, where California sea lions travel miles into the Pacific in search of seasonal, rich fishing grounds. Here, they join one of the open ocean's great feeding spectacles as black skipjack tuna, mahi-mahi and seabirds converge on vast schools of fish in a dramatic battle for a meal.
Some animals aren’t just visitors here; they spend their entire lives in this immense expanse. Rough-toothed dolphins have roamed the oceans since before woolly mammoths walked the earth, and yet we know very little about them. To help find food, they use sophisticated teamwork and ingenious hunting techniques that have rarely been witnessed.
Although the open ocean seems like a featureless expanse, it is shaped by powerful currents that flow across the globe like invisible rivers. These currents transport animals, nutrients and entire ecosystems across immense distances. For ocean drifters such as Smith's swimming crabs, the currents are both a lifeline and a gamble, carrying them through a world where danger can appear without warning.
Currents also drive one of the largest floating ecosystems on the planet. Today, the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt stretches over 5,000 miles across the ocean. But changing conditions are sweeping unprecedented amounts of this seaweed onto coastlines throughout the Caribbean. On the beaches of Mexico, turtle hatchlings emerging from their nests face a daunting new obstacle as mountains of sargassum block their path to the sea. Their struggle reveals how changes in the open ocean can have profound consequences far beyond the horizon.
In the Pacific, we follow one of nature's greatest aerial pirates, a frigatebird mother raising her chick alone.

programme.title: Blue Planet III
programme.desc:
The oceans have seasons just as the land does. Stretching across the temperate bands located between the freezing poles and the warm tropics lie the seasonal seas. Life is tough in these constantly changing waters, but if animals can persevere and adapt to change, there are myriad opportunities to not only survive but thrive here.
Winter in the seasonal seas is a battlefield. Storms whip up immense waves that can travel for thousands of miles, building to 30 metres in height before making landfall. On the Pacific coast of South America, such waves impact the lives of South America sea lions that have lived on this exposed coast for generations. Newborn pups and mothers are restricted to the colony, but the most intrepid males take a risk, leaving the tempestuous coast for unfamiliar waters and unusual prey - black-necked swans.
Some choose to escape, whilst others are undeterred by winters icy grip on the seasonal seas. In Patagonia, a female southern right whale arrives in the protected bay where she was likely born, in search of a mate. Testing prospective partners before accepting the best mate, she is rewarded with a gentle belly rub and embrace - a valuable pairing given that these animals were hunted to near extinction in the last century. The whaling ban increased this population from just 300 to 25,000, with a surprising twist – white calves.
As daylight lengthens and spring approaches, the greening of the seasonal seas commences. Plankton multiplies, creating huge blooms and feeding many species, including a rather peculiar crustacean, a porcelain crab. In the waters off Chile, over 200 million feast on this bounty, forming the largest-known aggregation of crabs in our oceans. But with limited space and an increased flow of plankton, the crabs do something remarkable - they organise themselves into structured lines, a behaviour that has never been filmed before.
As forests flourish on land, they also do so in the water. In spring, kelp, one of the fastest-growing organisms on earth, can lengthen by half a metre a day, forming submarine jungles that are home to a variety of creatures. In Japan, these lush fronds conceal a rarely seen fish, an eelpout, with a length of just ten centimetres.

In this episode, the experts lend their skills to a community project, hear the story behind a new treasure to be repaired and visit a local crafting hero.
Will and Dom are in Aberfeldy’s Crannog Centre, where visitors experience recreations of 5,000-year-old traditional dwellings. After a devastating fire three years ago put the project in jeopardy, thatcher Scott is looking to the future and building a new cookhouse, using traditional techniques and local materials. It could mean big business for the centre and increased opportunities to work with the local community, but creating Iron Age dwellings in the modern age is anything but simple.
Will then heads off to Scone Palace, crowning place of Scottish kings, to meet a couple with a family heirloom in need of rescue. It’s a handwritten Gaelic piping music book, handed down from Ian’s great-grandfather Donald, known as the Hero of Alma after his actions in the Crimean War. Now severely damaged, the music in its brittle pages might be lost forever if bookbinder Chris Shaw cannot bring it back from the brink. Ian will never play the songs it contains, as he has been battling motor neurone disease for the past decade, but he hopes if Chris Shaw is successful, the book can be passed down to his own son, also named Donald in honour of his ancestor.
Always in search of a new challenge, Dom joins a Perth-based family business whose handmade sporrans are the perfect accessory to Scotland’s famous kilts. It’s a critically endangered heritage craft that dates back to the 12th century, and the family is turning to technology to keep up with the challenge faced by cheaper, mass-produced versions made abroad. programme.title: Young, British and Tradwife
programme.desc:
Tradwives are trending. The term is in the dictionary, and the hashtag has over 300 million views on TikTok. Online tradwives promote the pleasures of domesticity and teach others how to be perfect homemakers in effortless and elegant social media videos that generate millions of likes. But they are not just an online phenomenon. Women in the real world, inspired by online influencers, are increasingly rejecting feminism, workplace hustle and hook-up culture to bake sourdough, homeschool the kids and obey their husbands.
BAFTA- and Grierson Award-nominated documentarian Poppy Jay wants to know why the tradwife world of domestic chores and submission appeals to so many. Reflecting on her own experience of forced marriage, she packs away her camera, pins on an apron and meets with British tradwives to find out if this is what true choice looks like in the 21st century.
As she juggles baking, sewing and schooling, she asks if a movement that demands submission to a husband is the solution to modern burnout or just the latest manifestation of an age-old misogynistic culture shaped by men, for men.
Poppy meets women from across the tradwife spectrum, from the newly married coach of ‘biblical wifery’ with 70,000 TikTok followers to the homeschooling mother of seven, to discover why the simple life rooted in traditional Christian values is suddenly so popular. Immersing herself in family life, Poppy challenges her own preconceptions, asking why any women would choose to submit to her husband and whether feminism has, as the tradwives claim, betrayed women by promising them they can have it all. programme.desc:
In this episode, the experts lend their skills to a community project, hear the story behind a new treasure to be repaired and visit a local crafting hero.
Will and Dom travel to Devon, and where better to find Daisy, the oversized fibreglass dairy cow lantern? She’s been a fixture at Hemyock Light Parade for a decade, but time hasn’t been kind to their bovine mascot. She’s lost an ear, a couple of hooves, and her body is dirty and cracked. It’s going to take some lateral thinking, and the skills of some exciting new experts, if she’s to take her place at the head of the parade once again.
In Poole, Will meets Ronnie, who has a musical instrument that reached the peak of its popularity in the 1920s and 1930s and which he would like fixed. It’s a banjolele that his father, part of the Windrush generation, brought from Jamaica to England. Most famously associated with George Formby, Ronnie’s mixture of banjo and ukulele is struggling to play a tune now, suffering from damage to the frets and a loose drum head. They’ll need to be fixed before luthier Julyan can even think about starting the cosmetic work required to the veneer.
Dom checks in on an old friend in Torquay. He’s at Dave Smith’s workshop, overlooking the harbour, to try his hand at the lost art of brilliant cutting before turning a newly decorated piece of glass into a Victorian-style mirror. As Dave can boast clients like David Beckham, John Meyer and Disney, it’s a rare chance for Dom to get some tips straight from a master craftsman. Fish and chips by the sea are an added bonus. programme.title: The Repair Shop on the Road
programme.sub-title: Ayrshire - Restoring Robert Burns Graffiti ║ S1
programme.desc:
Carpenter Will and horologist Steve are far from home today, exploring Ayrshire on Scotland’s west coast. Their first stop is the Scottish Boat Building School in Irvine, where Tom is waiting with a very unusual vessel. It’s a three-piece canoe designed in the 1930s and small enough to fit in the guard’s van of a train, which meant tourists could bring their own canoes on holiday in the years before owning a car was commonplace. It represents a different kind of freedom for Tom, though. His achondroplasia means a regular-size canoe is too difficult to manoeuvre. If this folding version can be fixed, he will finally have the freedom to take his daughter out exploring the waterways of Britain.
Ayrshire is the birthplace of Scotland’s national poet, Robert Burns, and many of the towns and villages in the region can boast strong links to his life and works. So it’s no surprise that when Will is called to Barr Castle in Galston, he comes face-to-face with a very special artefact. It’s a windowpane with a hand inscription by Robert Burns himself. However, it has suffered some damage in the past, so for decades its current custodians have had it hidden away in a cupboard for safekeeping. With the help of ceramics expert Kirsten Ramsay, they hope to once again put it on display. Fixing glass is notoriously difficult, and Kirsten definitely feels the pressure of getting such an important object looking back to its best.
While in the area, Steve takes the chance to visit Kays in Mauchline, who have been crafting curling stones for over 170 years. Using a dense granite quarried from a single Scottish island, these dedicated craftspeople hone stones of unparalleled quality for use in the Winter Olympics. Steve gets the chance to help with the process, but will it be gold, silver or bronze for his efforts? programme.title: MasterChef: The Professionals
programme.desc:
Five chefs remain in the race for a place in the quarter-final. But two more high-pressure challenges, which will test every aspect of their cooking, stand in their way.
Marcus and Monica are joined by special guest Adejoké Bakare, whose restaurant Chishuru is at the forefront of West African fine dining. In 2024, Adejoké became the first black woman in the UK to be awarded a coveted Michelin star. Now she’s setting the chefs a dish from her own repertoire: mushroom moin moin, served with a shito sauce and steamed egg.
It may sound simple, but this deceptively complex dish is packed with unfamiliar ingredients, techniques and flavours, and only one of the chefs has ever cooked moin moin before. With no recipe to follow, they’ll have to rely entirely on their palates, instincts and technical skills to recreate Adejoké’s dish. But with a place in the quarter-final on the line, get it wrong and the consequences could be huge.
Next up, it all comes down to dessert. The chefs have one last opportunity to convince Marcus and Monica that they deserve to stay in the competition.
But pastry is an unforgiving business. Every element must be precise, every second counts, and even the smallest mistake can unravel a dish. The judges want more than technical perfection… they’re looking for personality, originality, and a dessert that leaves a lasting impression. Who can hold their nerve when it matters most? programme.title: BBC New Comedy Awards
programme.desc:
The BBC’s biggest comedy talent search has reached its final night. Almost 1,000 comedians applied to this year’s New Comedy Awards. More than 100 went head-to-head at showcases across the country, and just 30 made it through to the knockout heats. Now only six remain.
The finalists take to the stage one last time, each hoping to win over the judges and be crowned BBC New Comedian 2026.
The grand final is filmed in front of a full house at Birmingham’s iconic Town Hall. Presenting the night is award-winning writer, comedian and Hollywood actor Guz Khan, who made the journey from stand-up to the screen and knows exactly what the night means to the acts waiting in the wings.
Leading the judging panel is the multitalented and multi-award-winning comedian, actor and writer Amy Gledhill. Joining her are Kiell Smith-Bynoe, star of Ghosts and Taskmaster, and Dan Tiernan, a former BBC New Comedy Awards winner. Together, they weigh up the writing, the delivery and the originality of every act before choosing their winner.
Rounding off the night is a very special performance from last year’s winner, Eli Hart, who returns to hand over the award to this year’s champion.
The winner will receive a paid commission to write and perform their own 30-minute audio pilot under the mentorship of a BBC comedy commissioner, plus a trophy and £1,000 in cash. For a comic at the start of their career, it is a rare opportunity that could open plenty of doors.
Now in their 30th year, the New Comedy Awards have helped launch the careers of comedy greats who regularly feature on our stages and screens, including Peter Kay, Lee Mack, Russell Howard, Romesh Ranganathan, Alan Carr, Sarah Millican, Josie Long and Joe Lycett.
The finalists are hoping to follow in their footsteps.
Six comics. One stage. One title. Who will be crowned BBC New Comedian 2026? programme.title: MasterChef: The Professionals
programme.desc:
It’s quarter-final time again as the standout chefs from this week’s heats come together for another battle in the kitchen. The stakes are higher, the challenges more demanding, and the judges’ expectations are greater than ever.
First up is the invention test, where the chefs must make a surprise ingredient the star of the show. This time, it’s saffron, one of the world’s most-prized spices, renowned for its distinctive aroma, delicate floral notes and rich golden hue. But its extraordinary character comes with a challenge. Too little and its subtle flavour can disappear, but too much or poorly handled and it can overwhelm a dish with bitterness. The chefs must find the perfect balance, using their creativity and instinct to showcase saffron at its best. With just 70 minutes to cook and serve, can they transform this precious ingredient into something truly exceptional?
Next, the chefs face one of their toughest tests yet, cooking a two-course menu for three of the country’s leading food writers and critics, Leyla Kazim, Xanthe Clay and David Ellis. These seasoned critics know what separates a competent chef from a potential star, and this is a chance for the competitors to demonstrate the depth of their talent, with dishes that combine outstanding flavour, technical skill and individuality.
Taking the critics’ feedback into account, Marcus and Monica must now decide who has done enough to secure a place in knockout week. With the competition entering its most demanding phase, only the chefs who consistently deliver at the highest level will remain in the race for the coveted crown. programme.title: Songs of Praise
programme.desc:
International Men’s Day was established in 1999 to highlight positive male role models and raise awareness of men’s health and wellbeing. Ahead of this year’s event, Sean Fletcher is in Leeds exploring what it means to be a man in modern society, and how faith, friendship and a sense of purpose can help men thrive in mind, body and spirit.
He meets rugby league legend Jamie Jones-Buchanan, now CEO of Leeds Rhinos, where he made 421 appearances, as well as representing England and Great Britain. Jamie reflects on growing up without a father figure in one of the UK’s most deprived areas, and how rugby and his Christian faith provided positive male role models, and a sense of belonging and purpose. He challenges stereotypes of the macho rugby player, and his passion for helping the next generation comes to life during a training session.
In the Welsh valleys, Pastor John Funnell reflects on the extraordinary number of young men joining his congregation. John left a highly paid career after becoming a Christian and moved to one of Europe’s most deprived communities. He explains how his church offers practical skills, mentoring, friendship and faith, helping men see that their past does not have to determine their future.
Back in Leeds, Sean meets Chris Sayburn, a minister and renowned worship leader who spent 12 years living with chronic pain following complications after spinal surgery. He tells Sean how exercise and faith have helped him rebuild his life and how a community of men became a lifeline.
With uplifting hymns and songs from around the UK.
1. Sweet Heart of Jesus - Leeds Cathedral 2. Amazing Grace - The Kingdom Choir 3. Facing a Task Unfinished - Lisburn Cathedral 4. Lord of All Hopefulness - Chris Sayburn and Friends 5. Firm Foundation (He Won't) - Alive Lincoln Central 6. programme.title: Blue Planet III
programme.desc:
The open ocean is the largest wilderness on earth. Covering more than half of the planet's surface, it appears at first glance to be an endless blue desert. Yet hidden here are some of the most extraordinary animals.
We uncover the surprising strategies, epic journeys and remarkable resilience that allows life to thrive here. From wandering predators and drifting castaways to giant whales and tiny turtle hatchlings, it is a world where life survives against the odds.
The journey begins far beyond the sight of land, where California sea lions travel miles into the Pacific in search of seasonal, rich fishing grounds. Here, they join one of the open ocean's great feeding spectacles as black skipjack tuna, mahi-mahi and seabirds converge on vast schools of fish in a dramatic battle for a meal.
Some animals aren’t just visitors here; they spend their entire lives in this immense expanse. Rough-toothed dolphins have roamed the oceans since before woolly mammoths walked the earth, and yet we know very little about them. To help find food, they use sophisticated teamwork and ingenious hunting techniques that have rarely been witnessed.
Although the open ocean seems like a featureless expanse, it is shaped by powerful currents that flow across the globe like invisible rivers. These currents transport animals, nutrients and entire ecosystems across immense distances. For ocean drifters such as Smith's swimming crabs, the currents are both a lifeline and a gamble, carrying them through a world where danger can appear without warning.
Currents also drive one of the largest floating ecosystems on the planet. Today, the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt stretches over 5,000 miles across the ocean. But changing conditions are sweeping unprecedented amounts of this seaweed onto coastlines throughout the Caribbean. On the beaches of Mexico, turtle hatchlings emerging from their nests face a daunting new obstacle as mountains of sargassum block their path to the sea. Their struggle reveals how changes in the open ocean can have profound consequences far beyond the horizon.
In the Pacific, we follow one of nature's greatest aerial pirates, a frigatebird mother raising her chick alone.

programme.title: Blue Planet III
programme.desc:
The oceans have seasons just as the land does. Stretching across the temperate bands located between the freezing poles and the warm tropics lie the seasonal seas. Life is tough in these constantly changing waters, but if animals can persevere and adapt to change, there are myriad opportunities to not only survive but thrive here.
Winter in the seasonal seas is a battlefield. Storms whip up immense waves that can travel for thousands of miles, building to 30 metres in height before making landfall. On the Pacific coast of South America, such waves impact the lives of South America sea lions that have lived on this exposed coast for generations. Newborn pups and mothers are restricted to the colony, but the most intrepid males take a risk, leaving the tempestuous coast for unfamiliar waters and unusual prey - black-necked swans.
Some choose to escape, whilst others are undeterred by winters icy grip on the seasonal seas. In Patagonia, a female southern right whale arrives in the protected bay where she was likely born, in search of a mate. Testing prospective partners before accepting the best mate, she is rewarded with a gentle belly rub and embrace - a valuable pairing given that these animals were hunted to near extinction in the last century. The whaling ban increased this population from just 300 to 25,000, with a surprising twist – white calves.
As daylight lengthens and spring approaches, the greening of the seasonal seas commences. Plankton multiplies, creating huge blooms and feeding many species, including a rather peculiar crustacean, a porcelain crab. In the waters off Chile, over 200 million feast on this bounty, forming the largest-known aggregation of crabs in our oceans. But with limited space and an increased flow of plankton, the crabs do something remarkable - they organise themselves into structured lines, a behaviour that has never been filmed before.
As forests flourish on land, they also do so in the water. In spring, kelp, one of the fastest-growing organisms on earth, can lengthen by half a metre a day, forming submarine jungles that are home to a variety of creatures. In Japan, these lush fronds conceal a rarely seen fish, an eelpout, with a length of just ten centimetres.

programme.title: The Repair Shop on the Road
programme.sub-title: Perthshire - Rebuilding an Ancient Settlement ║ S1
programme.desc:
In this episode, the experts lend their skills to a community project, hear the story behind a new treasure to be repaired and visit a local crafting hero.
Will and Dom are in Aberfeldy’s Crannog Centre, where visitors experience recreations of 5,000-year-old traditional dwellings. After a devastating fire three years ago put the project in jeopardy, thatcher Scott is looking to the future and building a new cookhouse, using traditional techniques and local materials. It could mean big business for the centre and increased opportunities to work with the local community, but creating Iron Age dwellings in the modern age is anything but simple.
Will then heads off to Scone Palace, crowning place of Scottish kings, to meet a couple with a family heirloom in need of rescue. It’s a handwritten Gaelic piping music book, handed down from Ian’s great-grandfather Donald, known as the Hero of Alma after his actions in the Crimean War. Now severely damaged, the music in its brittle pages might be lost forever if bookbinder Chris Shaw cannot bring it back from the brink. Ian will never play the songs it contains, as he has been battling motor neurone disease for the past decade, but he hopes if Chris Shaw is successful, the book can be passed down to his own son, also named Donald in honour of his ancestor.
Always in search of a new challenge, Dom joins a Perth-based family business whose handmade sporrans are the perfect accessory to Scotland’s famous kilts. It’s a critically endangered heritage craft that dates back to the 12th century, and the family is turning to technology to keep up with the challenge faced by cheaper, mass-produced versions made abroad. Dom is always eager to get on the tools, so what will his hosts make of his attempts at leatherworking? programme.title: Young, British and Tradwife
programme.desc:
Tradwives are trending. The term is in the dictionary, and the hashtag has over 300 million views on TikTok. Online tradwives promote the pleasures of domesticity and teach others how to be perfect homemakers in effortless and elegant social media videos that generate millions of likes. But they are not just an online phenomenon. Women in the real world, inspired by online influencers, are increasingly rejecting feminism, workplace hustle and hook-up culture to bake sourdough, homeschool the kids and obey their husbands.
BAFTA- and Grierson Award-nominated documentarian Poppy Jay wants to know why the tradwife world of domestic chores and submission appeals to so many. Reflecting on her own experience of forced marriage, she packs away her camera, pins on an apron and meets with British tradwives to find out if this is what true choice looks like in the 21st century.
As she juggles baking, sewing and schooling, she asks if a movement that demands submission to a husband is the solution to modern burnout or just the latest manifestation of an age-old misogynistic culture shaped by men, for men.
Poppy meets women from across the tradwife spectrum, from the newly married coach of ‘biblical wifery’ with 70,000 TikTok followers to the homeschooling mother of seven, to discover why the simple life rooted in traditional Christian values is suddenly so popular. Immersing herself in family life, Poppy challenges her own preconceptions, asking why any women would choose to submit to her husband and whether feminism has, as the tradwives claim, betrayed women by promising them they can have it all. In this episode, the experts lend their skills to a community project, hear the story behind a new treasure to be repaired and visit a local crafting hero.
Will and Dom travel to Devon, and where better to find Daisy, the oversized fibreglass dairy cow lantern? She’s been a fixture at Hemyock Light Parade for a decade, but time hasn’t been kind to their bovine mascot. She’s lost an ear, a couple of hooves, and her body is dirty and cracked. It’s going to take some lateral thinking, and the skills of some exciting new experts, if she’s to take her place at the head of the parade once again.
In Poole, Will meets Ronnie, who has a musical instrument that reached the peak of its popularity in the 1920s and 1930s and which he would like fixed. It’s a banjolele that his father, part of the Windrush generation, brought from Jamaica to England. Most famously associated with George Formby, Ronnie’s mixture of banjo and ukulele is struggling to play a tune now, suffering from damage to the frets and a loose drum head. They’ll need to be fixed before luthier Julyan can even think about starting the cosmetic work required to the veneer.
Dom checks in on an old friend in Torquay. He’s at Dave Smith’s workshop, overlooking the harbour, to try his hand at the lost art of brilliant cutting before turning a newly decorated piece of glass into a Victorian-style mirror. As Dave can boast clients like David Beckham, John Meyer and Disney, it’s a rare chance for Dom to get some tips straight from a master craftsman. Fish and chips by the sea are an added bonus. programme.title: The Repair Shop on the Road
programme.sub-title: Ayrshire - Restoring Robert Burns Graffiti ║ S1
programme.desc:
Carpenter Will and horologist Steve are far from home today, exploring Ayrshire on Scotland’s west coast. Their first stop is the Scottish Boat Building School in Irvine, where Tom is waiting with a very unusual vessel. It’s a three-piece canoe designed in the 1930s and small enough to fit in the guard’s van of a train, which meant tourists could bring their own canoes on holiday in the years before owning a car was commonplace. It represents a different kind of freedom for Tom, though. His achondroplasia means a regular-size canoe is too difficult to manoeuvre. If this folding version can be fixed, he will finally have the freedom to take his daughter out exploring the waterways of Britain.
Ayrshire is the birthplace of Scotland’s national poet, Robert Burns, and many of the towns and villages in the region can boast strong links to his life and works. So it’s no surprise that when Will is called to Barr Castle in Galston, he comes face-to-face with a very special artefact. It’s a windowpane with a hand inscription by Robert Burns himself. However, it has suffered some damage in the past, so for decades its current custodians have had it hidden away in a cupboard for safekeeping. With the help of ceramics expert Kirsten Ramsay, they hope to once again put it on display. Fixing glass is notoriously difficult, and Kirsten definitely feels the pressure of getting such an important object looking back to its best.
While in the area, Steve takes the chance to visit Kays in Mauchline, who have been crafting curling stones for over 170 years. Using a dense granite quarried from a single Scottish island, these dedicated craftspeople hone stones of unparalleled quality for use in the Winter Olympics. Steve gets the chance to help with the process, but will it be gold, silver or bronze for his efforts? programme.title: MasterChef: The Professionals
programme.desc:
Five chefs remain in the race for a place in the quarter-final. But two more high-pressure challenges, which will test every aspect of their cooking, stand in their way.
Marcus and Monica are joined by special guest Adejoké Bakare, whose restaurant Chishuru is at the forefront of West African fine dining. In 2024, Adejoké became the first black woman in the UK to be awarded a coveted Michelin star. Now she’s setting the chefs a dish from her own repertoire: mushroom moin moin, served with a shito sauce and steamed egg.
It may sound simple, but this deceptively complex dish is packed with unfamiliar ingredients, techniques and flavours, and only one of the chefs has ever cooked moin moin before. With no recipe to follow, they’ll have to rely entirely on their palates, instincts and technical skills to recreate Adejoké’s dish. But with a place in the quarter-final on the line, get it wrong and the consequences could be huge.
Next up, it all comes down to dessert. The chefs have one last opportunity to convince Marcus and Monica that they deserve to stay in the competition.
But pastry is an unforgiving business. Every element must be precise, every second counts, and even the smallest mistake can unravel a dish. The judges want more than technical perfection… they’re looking for personality, originality, and a dessert that leaves a lasting impression. Who can hold their nerve when it matters most? programme.title: BBC New Comedy Awards
programme.desc:
The BBC’s biggest comedy talent search has reached its final night. Almost 1,000 comedians applied to this year’s New Comedy Awards. More than 100 went head-to-head at showcases across the country, and just 30 made it through to the knockout heats. Now only six remain.
The finalists take to the stage one last time, each hoping to win over the judges and be crowned BBC New Comedian 2026.
The grand final is filmed in front of a full house at Birmingham’s iconic Town Hall. Presenting the night is award-winning writer, comedian and Hollywood actor Guz Khan, who made the journey from stand-up to the screen and knows exactly what the night means to the acts waiting in the wings.
Leading the judging panel is the multitalented and multi-award-winning comedian, actor and writer Amy Gledhill. Joining her are Kiell Smith-Bynoe, star of Ghosts and Taskmaster, and Dan Tiernan, a former BBC New Comedy Awards winner. Together, they weigh up the writing, the delivery and the originality of every act before choosing their winner.
Rounding off the night is a very special performance from last year’s winner, Eli Hart, who returns to hand over the award to this year’s champion.
The winner will receive a paid commission to write and perform their own 30-minute audio pilot under the mentorship of a BBC comedy commissioner, plus a trophy and £1,000 in cash. For a comic at the start of their career, it is a rare opportunity that could open plenty of doors.
Now in their 30th year, the New Comedy Awards have helped launch the careers of comedy greats who regularly feature on our stages and screens, including Peter Kay, Lee Mack, Russell Howard, Romesh Ranganathan, Alan Carr, Sarah Millican, Josie Long and Joe Lycett.
The finalists are hoping to follow in their footsteps.
Six comics. One stage. One title. Who will be crowned BBC New Comedian 2026? programme.title: MasterChef: The Professionals
programme.desc:
It’s quarter-final time again as the standout chefs from this week’s heats come together for another battle in the kitchen. The stakes are higher, the challenges more demanding, and the judges’ expectations are greater than ever.
First up is the invention test, where the chefs must make a surprise ingredient the star of the show. This time, it’s saffron, one of the world’s most-prized spices, renowned for its distinctive aroma, delicate floral notes and rich golden hue. But its extraordinary character comes with a challenge. Too little and its subtle flavour can disappear, but too much or poorly handled and it can overwhelm a dish with bitterness. The chefs must find the perfect balance, using their creativity and instinct to showcase saffron at its best. With just 70 minutes to cook and serve, can they transform this precious ingredient into something truly exceptional?
Next, the chefs face one of their toughest tests yet, cooking a two-course menu for three of the country’s leading food writers and critics, Leyla Kazim, Xanthe Clay and David Ellis. These seasoned critics know what separates a competent chef from a potential star, and this is a chance for the competitors to demonstrate the depth of their talent, with dishes that combine outstanding flavour, technical skill and individuality.
Taking the critics’ feedback into account, Marcus and Monica must now decide who has done enough to secure a place in knockout week. With the competition entering its most demanding phase, only the chefs who consistently deliver at the highest level will remain in the race for the coveted crown. programme.title: Songs of Praise
programme.desc:
International Men’s Day was established in 1999 to highlight positive male role models and raise awareness of men’s health and wellbeing. Ahead of this year’s event, Sean Fletcher is in Leeds exploring what it means to be a man in modern society, and how faith, friendship and a sense of purpose can help men thrive in mind, body and spirit.
He meets rugby league legend Jamie Jones-Buchanan, now CEO of Leeds Rhinos, where he made 421 appearances, as well as representing England and Great Britain. Jamie reflects on growing up without a father figure in one of the UK’s most deprived areas, and how rugby and his Christian faith provided positive male role models, and a sense of belonging and purpose. He challenges stereotypes of the macho rugby player, and his passion for helping the next generation comes to life during a training session.
In the Welsh valleys, Pastor John Funnell reflects on the extraordinary number of young men joining his congregation. John left a highly paid career after becoming a Christian and moved to one of Europe’s most deprived communities. He explains how his church offers practical skills, mentoring, friendship and faith, helping men see that their past does not have to determine their future.
Back in Leeds, Sean meets Chris Sayburn, a minister and renowned worship leader who spent 12 years living with chronic pain following complications after spinal surgery. He tells Sean how exercise and faith have helped him rebuild his life and how a community of men became a lifeline.
With uplifting hymns and songs from around the UK.

programme.title: Blue Planet III
programme.desc:
The open ocean is the largest wilderness on earth. Covering more than half of the planet's surface, it appears at first glance to be an endless blue desert. Yet hidden here are some of the most extraordinary animals.
We uncover the surprising strategies, epic journeys and remarkable resilience that allows life to thrive here. From wandering predators and drifting castaways to giant whales and tiny turtle hatchlings, it is a world where life survives against the odds.
The journey begins far beyond the sight of land, where California sea lions travel miles into the Pacific in search of seasonal, rich fishing grounds. Here, they join one of the open ocean's great feeding spectacles as black skipjack tuna, mahi-mahi and seabirds converge on vast schools of fish in a dramatic battle for a meal.
Some animals aren’t just visitors here; they spend their entire lives in this immense expanse. Rough-toothed dolphins have roamed the oceans since before woolly mammoths walked the earth, and yet we know very little about them. To help find food, they use sophisticated teamwork and ingenious hunting techniques that have rarely been witnessed.
Although the open ocean seems like a featureless expanse, it is shaped by powerful currents that flow across the globe like invisible rivers. These currents transport animals, nutrients and entire ecosystems across immense distances. For ocean drifters such as Smith's swimming crabs, the currents are both a lifeline and a gamble, carrying them through a world where danger can appear without warning.
Currents also drive one of the largest floating ecosystems on the planet. Today, the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt stretches over 5,000 miles across the ocean. But changing conditions are sweeping unprecedented amounts of this seaweed onto coastlines throughout the Caribbean. On the beaches of Mexico, turtle hatchlings emerging from their nests face a daunting new obstacle as mountains of sargassum block their path to the sea. Their struggle reveals how changes in the open ocean can have profound consequences far beyond the horizon.
In the Pacific, we follow one of nature's greatest aerial pirates, a frigatebird mother raising her chick alone.

programme.title: Blue Planet III
programme.desc:
The oceans have seasons just as the land does. Stretching across the temperate bands located between the freezing poles and the warm tropics lie the seasonal seas. Life is tough in these constantly changing waters, but if animals can persevere and adapt to change, there are myriad opportunities to not only survive but thrive here.
Winter in the seasonal seas is a battlefield. Storms whip up immense waves that can travel for thousands of miles, building to 30 metres in height before making landfall. On the Pacific coast of South America, such waves impact the lives of South America sea lions that have lived on this exposed coast for generations. Newborn pups and mothers are restricted to the colony, but the most intrepid males take a risk, leaving the tempestuous coast for unfamiliar waters and unusual prey - black-necked swans.
Some choose to escape, whilst others are undeterred by winters icy grip on the seasonal seas. In Patagonia, a female southern right whale arrives in the protected bay where she was likely born, in search of a mate. Testing prospective partners before accepting the best mate, she is rewarded with a gentle belly rub and embrace - a valuable pairing given that these animals were hunted to near extinction in the last century. The whaling ban increased this population from just 300 to 25,000, with a surprising twist – white calves.
As daylight lengthens and spring approaches, the greening of the seasonal seas commences. Plankton multiplies, creating huge blooms and feeding many species, including a rather peculiar crustacean, a porcelain crab. In the waters off Chile, over 200 million feast on this bounty, forming the largest-known aggregation of crabs in our oceans. But with limited space and an increased flow of plankton, the crabs do something remarkable - they organise themselves into structured lines, a behaviour that has never been filmed before.
As forests flourish on land, they also do so in the water. In spring, kelp, one of the fastest-growing organisms on earth, can lengthen by half a metre a day, forming submarine jungles that are home to a variety of creatures. In Japan, these lush fronds conceal a rarely seen fish, an eelpout, with a length of just ten centimetres.

In this episode, the experts lend their skills to a community project, hear the story behind a new treasure to be repaired and visit a local crafting hero.
Will and Dom are in Aberfeldy’s Crannog Centre, where visitors experience recreations of 5,000-year-old traditional dwellings. It’s a handwritten Gaelic piping music book, handed down from Ian’s great-grandfather Donald, known as the Hero of Alma after his actions in the Crimean War. Now severely damaged, the music in its brittle pages might be lost forever if bookbinder Chris Shaw cannot bring it back from the brink. Ian will never play the songs it contains, as he has been battling motor neurone disease for the past decade, but he hopes if Chris Shaw is successful, the book can be passed down to his own son, also named Donald in honour of his ancestor.
Always in search of a new challenge, Dom joins a Perth-based family business whose handmade sporrans are the perfect accessory to Scotland’s famous kilts. It’s a critically endangered heritage craft that dates back to the 12th century, and the family is turning to technology to keep up with the challenge faced by cheaper, mass-produced versions made abroad. programme.title: Young, British and Tradwife
programme.desc:
Tradwives are trending. The term is in the dictionary, and the hashtag has over 300 million views on TikTok. Online tradwives promote the pleasures of domesticity and teach others how to be perfect homemakers in effortless and elegant social media videos that generate millions of likes. But they are not just an online phenomenon. Women in the real world, inspired by online influencers, are increasingly rejecting feminism, workplace hustle and hook-up culture to bake sourdough, homeschool the kids and obey their husbands.
BAFTA- and Grierson Award-nominated documentarian Poppy Jay wants to know why the tradwife world of domestic chores and submission appeals to so many. Reflecting on her own experience of forced marriage, she packs away her camera, pins on an apron and meets with British tradwives to find out if this is what true choice looks like in the 21st century.
As she juggles baking, sewing and schooling, she asks if a movement that demands submission to a husband is the solution to modern burnout or just the latest manifestation of an age-old misogynistic culture shaped by men, for men.
Poppy meets women from across the tradwife spectrum, from the newly married coach of ‘biblical wifery’ with 70,000 TikTok followers to the homeschooling mother of seven, to discover why the simple life rooted in traditional Christian values is suddenly so popular. Immersing herself in family life, Poppy challenges her own preconceptions, asking why any women would choose to submit to her husband and whether feminism has, as the tradwives claim, betrayed women by promising them they can have it all. In this episode, the experts lend their skills to a community project, hear the story behind a new treasure to be repaired and visit a local crafting hero.
Will and Dom travel to Devon, and where better to find Daisy, the oversized fibreglass dairy cow lantern? She’s been a fixture at Hemyock Light Parade for a decade, but time hasn’t been kind to their bovine mascot. She’s lost an ear, a couple of hooves, and her body is dirty and cracked. It’s going to take some lateral thinking, and the skills of some exciting new experts, if she’s to take her place at the head of the parade once again.
In Poole, Will meets Ronnie, who has a musical instrument that reached the peak of its popularity in the 1920s and 1930s and which he would like fixed. It’s a banjolele that his father, part of the Windrush generation, brought from Jamaica to England. Most famously associated with George Formby, Ronnie’s mixture of banjo and ukulele is struggling to play a tune now, suffering from damage to the frets and a loose drum head. They’ll need to be fixed before luthier Julyan can even think about starting the cosmetic work required to the veneer.
Dom checks in on an old friend in Torquay. He’s at Dave Smith’s workshop, overlooking the harbour, to try his hand at the lost art of brilliant cutting before turning a newly decorated piece of glass into a Victorian-style mirror. As Dave can boast clients like David Beckham, John Meyer and Disney, it’s a rare chance for Dom to get some tips straight from a master craftsman. Fish and chips by the sea are an added bonus. programme.title: The Repair Shop on the Road
programme.sub-title: Ayrshire - Restoring Robert Burns Graffiti ║ S1
programme.desc:
Carpenter Will and horologist Steve are far from home today, exploring Ayrshire on Scotland’s west coast. Their first stop is the Scottish Boat Building School in Irvine, where Tom is waiting with a very unusual vessel. It’s a three-piece canoe designed in the 1930s and small enough to fit in the guard’s van of a train, which meant tourists could bring their own canoes on holiday in the years before owning a car was commonplace. It represents a different kind of freedom for Tom, though. His achondroplasia means a regular-size canoe is too difficult to manoeuvre. If this folding version can be fixed, he will finally have the freedom to take his daughter out exploring the waterways of Britain.
Ayrshire is the birthplace of Scotland’s national poet, Robert Burns, and many of the towns and villages in the region can boast strong links to his life and works. So it’s no surprise that when Will is called to Barr Castle in Galston, he comes face-to-face with a very special artefact. It’s a windowpane with a hand inscription by Robert Burns himself. However, it has suffered some damage in the past, so for decades its current custodians have had it hidden away in a cupboard for safekeeping. With the help of ceramics expert Kirsten Ramsay, they hope to once again put it on display. Fixing glass is notoriously difficult, and Kirsten definitely feels the pressure of getting such an important object looking back to its best.
While in the area, Steve takes the chance to visit Kays in Mauchline, who have been crafting curling stones for over 170 years. Using a dense granite quarried from a single Scottish island, these dedicated craftspeople hone stones of unparalleled quality for use in the Winter Olympics. Steve gets the chance to help with the process, but will it be gold, silver or bronze for his efforts? programme.title: MasterChef: The Professionals
programme.desc:
Five chefs remain in the race for a place in the quarter-final. But two more high-pressure challenges, which will test every aspect of their cooking, stand in their way.
Marcus and Monica are joined by special guest Adejoké Bakare, whose restaurant Chishuru is at the forefront of West African fine dining. In 2024, Adejoké became the first black woman in the UK to be awarded a coveted Michelin star. Now she’s setting the chefs a dish from her own repertoire: mushroom moin moin, served with a shito sauce and steamed egg.
It may sound simple, but this deceptively complex dish is packed with unfamiliar ingredients, techniques and flavours, and only one of the chefs has ever cooked moin moin before. With no recipe to follow, they’ll have to rely entirely on their palates, instincts and technical skills to recreate Adejoké’s dish. But with a place in the quarter-final on the line, get it wrong and the consequences could be huge.
Next up, it all comes down to dessert. The chefs have one last opportunity to convince Marcus and Monica that they deserve to stay in the competition.
But pastry is an unforgiving business. Every element must be precise, every second counts, and even the smallest mistake can unravel a dish. The judges want more than technical perfection… they’re looking for personality, originality, and a dessert that leaves a lasting impression. Who can hold their nerve when it matters most? programme.title: BBC New Comedy Awards
programme.desc:
The BBC’s biggest comedy talent search has reached its final night. Almost 1,000 comedians applied to this year’s New Comedy Awards. More than 100 went head-to-head at showcases across the country, and just 30 made it through to the knockout heats. Now only six remain.
The finalists take to the stage one last time, each hoping to win over the judges and be crowned BBC New Comedian 2026.
The grand final is filmed in front of a full house at Birmingham’s iconic Town Hall. Presenting the night is award-winning writer, comedian and Hollywood actor Guz Khan, who made the journey from stand-up to the screen and knows exactly what the night means to the acts waiting in the wings.
Leading the judging panel is the multitalented and multi-award-winning comedian, actor and writer Amy Gledhill. Joining her are Kiell Smith-Bynoe, star of Ghosts and Taskmaster, and Dan Tiernan, a former BBC New Comedy Awards winner. Together, they weigh up the writing, the delivery and the originality of every act before choosing their winner.
Rounding off the night is a very special performance from last year’s winner, Eli Hart, who returns to hand over the award to this year’s champion.
The winner will receive a paid commission to write and perform their own 30-minute audio pilot under the mentorship of a BBC comedy commissioner, plus a trophy and £1,000 in cash. For a comic at the start of their career, it is a rare opportunity that could open plenty of doors.
Now in their 30th year, the New Comedy Awards have helped launch the careers of comedy greats who regularly feature on our stages and screens, including Peter Kay, Lee Mack, Russell Howard, Romesh Ranganathan, Alan Carr, Sarah Millican, Josie Long and Joe Lycett.
The finalists are hoping to follow in their footsteps.
Six comics. One stage. One title. Who will be crowned BBC New Comedian 2026? programme.title: SpeakGaelic
programme.desc:
Tha Joy Dunlop a’ leantainn oirre ’s i gar toirt tro cheumannan a bharrachd ann a bhith ag ionnsachadh na Gàidhlig. Bidh i a’ dèiligeadh ri facail is abairtean air measgachadh de chuspairean làitheil agus, mar thè a dh’ionnsaich na Gàidhlig i fhèin, bheir Joy mìneachadh dhuinn air briathrachas, gràmar is gnathasan-cainnte ann an dòigh a tha furasta a thuigsinn.
Coinnichidh sinn ri luchd-labhairt èasgaidh a th’ air Gàidhlig ionnsachadh gu àrd ìre neo a thogadh leis a’ Ghàidhlig air falbh bho sgìrean traidiseanta na Gàidhealtachd, agus bidh Calum MacIlleathain a’ toirt sealladh dhuinn air annasan is cuspairean ’s e air chuairt air feadh na dùthcha.
Lorgar tuilleadh stuthan taic air-loidhne aig www.speakgaelic.scot, ann am pod-chraolaidhean SpeakGaelic air BBC Sounds agus tha na prògraman air fad rin lorg le fo-thiotalan air sianal YouTube SpeakGaelic.
Joy Dunlop guides viewers through the next steps to inspire us to keep on speaking Gaelic. As in previous series, she introduces and explains usage for words and phrases on everyday topics. A Gaelic learner herself, Joy supports us through vocabulary, grammar and idiom on topics such as medicine, politics, community and exercise.
Speakers who have embraced the language join in, and the intrepid Calum Maclean ventures to forgotten corners of Scotland seeking hidden treasures.
Supporting materials can be found online: www.speakgaelic.scot, in the SpeakGaelic podcasts on BBC Sounds and with English subtitles on SpeakGaelic’s YouTube channel. Presenter - Joy Dunlop Presenter - Calum Maclean Producer - Donald Macleod Executive Producer - Una McDonald.

programme.title: Cidsin Granaidh Chalanais
programme.desc:
Gregor MacLeod inherited his grannie’s old cookery book. In it she had written down over 50 recipes by hand and Gregor has set himself the challenge of cooking his way through them.
He takes on grannie’s version of gingerbread and her recipe for classic Scottish tablet. Gregor’s cousin Flora calls in to taste the gingerbread and she tells him of her memories of grannie making tablet at the stove.
To find out more about cooking in the family, he talks to his auntie Ann and borrows a pudding bowl from her. This will come in handy for grannie’s recipe for steamed apple dumpling. Shaking things up, Gregor takes grannie’s recipe for fishcakes and adds his own flair. He smokes his own fish over a bed of woodchips, herbs and pink peppercorns before flaking it through mashed potato to make the fishcakes. He serves them with his own home-made tartare sauce.
Fhuair Griogar MacLeòid seann leabhar còcaireachd a sheanmhair mar dhìleab: comhairle na làmh-sgrìobhaidh fhèin air còrr is lethcheud dinnear is greim blasta a dhèanamh. Tha Griogar a’ cur roimhe a’ dol tron a leabhar a’ feuchainn orra. Sa phrògram seo feuchaidh e dòigh a sheanmhair air aran dinnseir a dhèanamh, agus cuideachd suiteas tablet. Tha tè dhe chàirdean, Flòraidh, a’ tadhal a dh’fheuchainn na rinn e - tha deagh chuimhn’ aice-se air granaidh aig an stòbh. Cluinnidh e barrachd mu chòcaireachd san teaghlach bho Anna piuthar a’ mhàthar is gheibh e iasad bobhla mìlsein bhuaipe, a bhios math airson an duf ubhail aig granaidh a bhruich. Bheir e sùil air mar a rinn ise bonnaich èisg agus cuiridh e a dhreach fhèin orra. Smocaidh e an èisg os cionn grìosach fiodha, lusan is fras phìobair, ga mheasgadh an luib buntàta prann agus ga chur air an truinnsear le sabhs tartare a nì e fhèin. Presenter - Gregor Macleod Director - Ramsay MacMahon.

programme.title: Ro Thrath don t-Saoghal/Born too Soon
programme.desc:
Lean sgeulachdan teaghlaichean leanabain a rugadh ro thràth, agus na sgiobaidhean meidigeach a tha a’ coimhead às an dèidh, anns an t-sreath bhrosnachail làn-fhaireachdainn seo a bheir dhuinn sealladh farsaing air na daoine agus air an obair.
Air cùl dorsan Aonad Dlùth-chùram Leanabain Ospadal Mhàthraichean Oilthigh Chorcaigh ann an Èirinn, coinnichidh sinn ris na nursaichean, na dotairean agus na lannsairean fìor-adhartach a tha a’ dèanamh obair-lannsa do-chreidsinneach air naoidheanan a rugadh cho tràth ri còig seachdainean air fhichead, agus anns nach eil ach cuideam pacaid flùir.
Le caractaran brosnachail agus blàtha, chì sinn an dìcheall agus an gràdh a bheir an cothrom as fheàrr do leanabain a thàinig ro thràth, agus sinn a’ compàirteachadh anns an aoibhneas a tha an cois na ciad làithean aca san t-saoghal.
Follow the stories of families and medical teams looking after premature babies in an emotive and inspiring full-access series.
Go behind-the-scenes of the neo-natal unit at Cork University Maternity Hospital in Ireland and meet the nurses, doctors and pioneering surgeons performing incredible life-saving treatment on babies born as early as 25 weeks and weighing the same amount as a bag of flour.
With inspirational and heartwarming characters, witness the dedication and love put into giving babies born preterm the best chance possible, and share in the joy of their first days of life.
Dubbed in Gaelic with English subtitles.

programme.title: Sar Sgeoil
programme.desc:
Dracula, published in 1897, still endures as one of the best-known horror stories ever to be told. Bram Stoker’s character has horrified readers, and audiences, for over a century. Cathy Macdonald explores the Scottish connections to the writing of the novel. How did a vampire story by an Irish author, set in Transylvania and England, come to be written in Scotland and inspired by a Scot?
Stoker chose the small fishing village of Cruden Bay in the north east of Scotland to write much of the novel. Cathy explores why. She also finds out about Scot Emily Gerard, whose writings on Transylvanian superstitions were a huge influence for Stoker. Cathy also delves into some of the real history featured in the novel and visits the coastal town of Whitby, where Dracula first landed in Britain.
Nochd an leabhar Dracula aig Bram Stoker trì bliadhna ro dheireadh na naoitheamh linn deug – ach chun an là an diugh tha inbhe aige mar leabhar oillte cho ainmeil sa th’ann. Chuir Dracula uamhas air leughadairean fad còrr is ceud bliadhna. Tha Cathy Dhòmhnallach a’lorg na ceangail eadar Alba agus an leabhar. Ciamar a thachair e gun do sgrìobh Èireannach leabhar air iarrtaiche-fala, stèidhichte ann an Transylvania agus Sasainn, is e fhèin ann an Alba?
Roghnaich Stoker cuid dhen leabhar a’ sgrìobhadh ann am baile beag Bàgh Chrudain ann an ear-thuath na h-Alba. Cluinnidh Cathy carson, agus mun bhan-Albannach, Emily Gerard, is mun bhuaidh a bh’aig na sgrìobh ise mu bheul-aithris Transylvania air Stoker. Nì Cathy rannsachadh mun eachdraidh fhìrinneach a chaidh a shnìomh dhan leabhar – agus tadhlaidh i air baile Whitby, far an do chuir Dracula an toiseach cas air talamh Bhreatainn.
In Gaelic with English subtitles. Presenter - Cathy MacDonald Director - Julie McCrone.

programme.title: Bethany – An Dannsair Gaidhealach/The Highland Dancer
programme.desc:
Tha amasan mòr aig an dannsair òg Bethany, a tha aon bliadhna deug a dh’ aois, às na h-Eileanan Iar de dh’ Alba. Chaidh a togail ann an teaghlach làn dhannsairean Gàidhealach, agus tha Bethany cinnteach gu bheil i dol a leantainn ann an ceumannan a màthar agus peathraichean a màthar. Is dòcha gu bheil tàlantan dannsa a’ ruith anns an teaghlach, ach ’s e cho dìcheallach agus cho misneachail a dhearbhas ciamar a thèid dhi.
’S e stoidhle dannsa traidiseanta Albannach a th’ ann an dannsa gàidhealach agus ’s e barrachd air ealain a th’ ann, feumar neart agus dìcheall. ’S e seann dhannsa cogaidh a th’ ann an dannsa a’ chlaidheimh a bh’ air a dhannsa uaireigin ro bhlàran le ceatharnaich gàidhealach agus bha e air fhaicinn mar deagh fhortan nan cuireamaid crìoch air an dannsa gun suathadh anns na claidheamhan.
Tha Bethany òg a’ cur dùbhlan duilich roimhpe fhèin: a bhith a’ dèanamh aon de na dannsaichean as dorra a th’ ann, dannsa a’ chlaidheimh, aig prìomh fharpais ann an Steòrnabhagh, a’ dèanamh ceumannan nach eil i air a dhannsa a-riamh ron seo. An cuir Bethany crìoch air an dùbhlan aice gus na ceumannan duilich ionnsachadh ron fharpais agus am faigh i air an dannsa a dhèanamh gu grinn gus àite fhaighinn agus bonn a chosnadh?
Eleven-year-old Bethany is a young dancer from the Outer Hebrides of Scotland with big dreams. Born into a family of Highland dancers, Bethany is determined to follow in the footsteps of her mum and aunties. Dancing talent may run in the family, but dedication, courage and perseverance will determine her journey.
Highland dancing, a Scottish traditional style of dance, is more than just an art form and requires strength and stamina. The sword dance, an ancient act of war, was once performed by Highland warriors before battle and was considered a good omen if the dance was completed without touching the swords.
Bethany sets herself a daunting challenge - performing the notoriously difficult sword dance at a major Highland dancing competition in Stornoway, with steps she’s never been brave enough to try in competition before. Will Bethany complete her challenge and learn the complex dance steps in time for the contest, and will she manage to be placed and gain a medal?

Tha Bitzer air crìoch a chuir air an obair-taighe gu lèir agus a-nis chan eil càil aige ri dhèanamh. The e air a dhòigh nuair a mhothachas e gu bheil an t-sabhal feumach air sgioblachadh - gus an tig e tairsinn air dealbh nach gabh a chrochadh gu dìreach!
Bitzer has completed all his chores and is at a bit of a loss. He's delighted when he discovers the flock's barn needs a good tidy-up, until he comes across a wonky picture that just won't hang straight.

programme.desc: Ceòl agus còmhradh le Cathy Ann Nic a Phi còmhla ri Cairistiona Cheannadach. Music and chat programme presented by Cathy Ann MacPhee with guest Kristine Kennedy.

programme.title: Gàrraidhean Mòra na h-Alba
programme.desc:
Green-fingered Murdo Macdonald visits some of the country’s most important gardens to explore their design, plant-life, setting and history.
He visits the Japanese Garden at Cowden near Stirling and finds out about the two women who created the garden at the turn of the 20th century - Ella Christie and Taki Handa. The garden was badly vandalised in the 1960s, so Ella’s great, great niece tells Murdo what was involved in reconstructing the area. He also learns more about the cultural significance of the Japanese design of the garden.
Roddy Maclean tells us about the importance of moss and Dr Mark Newman of The Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh explains why trees turn such beautiful colours in the autumn.
Tha gàirneilear sgileil, Murchadh Dòmhnallach, a’ tadhal air cuid de ghàrraidhean mòra na h-Alba, a’coimhead air an cruth, na tha fàs unnta agus an eachdraidh.
Sa phrògram seo tha Murchadh a’tadhal air Gàrradh Siapanach Cowden, aig Dollar faisg air Sruighlea. Cluinnidh e mun dithis bhoirionnach a chruthaich e, tràth san fhicheadamh linn, Ella Christie agus Taki Handa. Rinn eucoraich droch mhilleadh air a’ghàrradh sna trì ficheadan, agus innsidh iar-ogha bràthair Ella Christie do Mhurchadh mun t-saothair a bh’aca ga chruthachadh as ùr. Gheibh e mach cuideachd cho cudromach sa tha cruth is cumadh gàrraidh ann an dualchas Siapan.
Innsidh Ruairidh MacIlleathain dhuinn cho cudromach sa tha còinneach, agus mìnichidh an t-Oll. Mark Newman bho Ghàrradh Luibheanach Rìoghail Dhùn-Èidinn dè’s coireach gu bheil duilleach nan craobh ag atharrachadh dath as t-fhoghar.
In Gaelic with English subtitles Presenter - Murdo Macdonald Producer - Julie McCrone.

programme.title: Mas Fhior
programme.desc:
Farpais-cheist do-chreidsinneach... Mas Fhìor! Le ochdnar Mas Fhìoraich a’ cluich bhon dachaighean fhèin, ’s iad an fheadhainn a chuireas na ceistean agus na freagairtean. An urrainn do Isla is Hamish agus Jamie is Liam a tha a’ cluich bhon stiùideo a’ chùis a dhèanamh orra airson an duais mhòr a bhuannachadh?
A quiz show that is pretty unbelievable! Eight Pretenders play from the comfort of their own homes and hold all the questions and answers to this quiz. Can Isla and Hamish, or Jamie and Liam in the studio beat the Pretenders for a chance to win a cash prize?
In Gaelic with English subtitles.

programme.title: Steelmen
programme.desc:
Ann an 1991, bha baile Thobar na Màthar a’ greimeachadh ris a’ bhuaidh shòisealta, eaconamach agus chultarail a bheireadh dùnadh ionad stàilinn Ravenscraig air an sgìre, ach airson a’ chiad uair ann an 39 bliadhna thog sgioba ball-coise a’ bhaile, na ‘Steelmen' mar a theirear riutha, Cupa na h-Alba, a’ toirt boillsgeadh dòchais a thogadh an dorchadas.
In 1991, as the town of Motherwell faced the crippling social, economic and cultural impact of the closure of the Ravenscraig steelworks, its football club, locally known as the Steelmen, lifted the prestigious Scottish Cup for the first time in 39 years. The victory was a glimmer of light in the ensuing darkness. Narrator - Alex O'Henley Executive Producer - Margot McCuaig Executive Producer - Iseabail Mactaggart.

programme.title: Ciad-fàthan nan Creutairean/Wild Senses
programme.desc:
’S caomh leinn a bhith smaoineachadh gu bheil eòlas againn air an t-saoghal timcheall oirnn, ach dè ma tha sinn dìreach a’ faicinn pàirt dheth? Tha Ciad-fàthan nan Creutairean a’ toirt cuireadh dhuinn coiseachd, snàmh agus leum am measg nam beathaichean agus an saoghal aca a thuigsinn nan àrainneachd fhèin.
Thairis air ceithir eapasodan iongantach, tha sinn ag ionnsachadh mu chiad-fàthan cumhachdach nam beathaichean, bho fradharc buileach mionaideach gu iasg a tha a’ blasad len craiceann. Faic mar a tha tìgearan gan cleith fhèin le bhith a’ cleachdadh an dath orains, mar a tha leumadairean a’ seòladh a’ chuain le echo-location, mathain-nighe a’ dèanamh an slighe le spògan air leth faireachail, agus tha fiù ’s craobhan a’ cur a-mach rabhaidhean ceimigeach.
Tha Ciad-fàthan nan Creutairean a’ taisbeanadh taobhan falaichte de nàdar - cailèideascop de chiad-fàthan nach eil sinn ach air tòiseachadh a’ tuigsinn.
We like to think we know the world around us, but what if we’re only seeing part of the picture? Wild Senses invites you to walk, swim or leap in someone else’s paws, fins or wings - and experience life from a wild perspective.
Across four mind-blowing episodes, we uncover animal supersenses, from high-resolution vision to fish that taste with their skin. Discover how tigers turn orange into camouflage, dolphins navigate the deep using echolocation, raccoons feel their way with hyper-sensitive paws, and even trees send out chemical alarms. The series reveals the hidden side of nature - a kaleidoscope of sensations we’re only just beginning to understand.
Dubbed in Gaelic with English subtitles.

programme.title: Skipinnish Aig A' Chaisteal
programme.desc:
Skipinnish le The Island ann an cuideachd na mìltean de luchd-leantainn aig cuirm-chiùil a’ comharrachadh 25 bliadhna de Skipinnish, bho Chaisteal Dhùn Èideann.
Skipinnish perform The Island in front of thousands of fans at a concert celebrating 25 years of the band, from Edinburgh Castle.

Air fhilmeadh aig àm Celtic Connections 2024 agus a’ taisbeanaidh chlàraidhean is chòmhraidhean a chaidh a dhèanamh a dh’aona ghothach airson Seirm, chìte cuid den luchd-ciùil a b’ fheàrr a bha aig an fhèis, leithid Kathryn Tickell & The Darkening, Eòghann MacEunraig, Genticorum, TEUD & Kaïa Kater.
Traditional and roots music show presented by Mary Ann Kennedy. Filmed during Celtic Connections 2024, Seirm showcases bespoke recordings and conversations with some of the best artists appearing at the festival. This episode features performances from Kathryn Tickell & The Darkening, Ewen Henderson, Genticorum and intimate session recordings with TEUD & Kaïa Kater.
In Gaelic with English subtitles. Presenter - Mary Ann Kennedy Executive Producer - Alasdair MacCuish Series Producer - Ewan Duncan Director - Iain Macleod Production Manager - Gillian MacLean.

programme.title: Scottish Women's Premier League (BBC ALBA)
programme.desc:
An dearbaidh Dhùn Èideann eadar Hearts agus Hibernian à Tynecastle beò air BBC ALBA. An geama slàn ri fhaicinn le aithris bho Donna NicNeill.
The Edinburgh derby at Tynecastle as Hearts take on Hibernian live on BBC ALBA. Full match coverage with commentary from Donna MacNeill.

programme.title: Abadas
programme.desc:
Tha na h-Abadas air bothan a dhèanamh anns an taigh agus a' faighinn tòrr spòrs bho bhith cluich anns an uisge. Tha facal an là-an-diugh co-cheangailte ri cumail tioram, cuideachd. Dè th'ann agus càite an lorg iad e?
The Abadas have made a den inside the house and are having a lot of fun playing in the rain. Today's word has something to do with keeping dry, too. What could it be and where will they find it?

programme.title: Pompon Am Mathan Beag/Pompon Little Bear
programme.desc:
Nuair a tha Pompon 's a phàrantan ag ullachadh 'son turas air falbh, feumaidh Pompon tighinn gu co-dhùnadh air dè tha riatanach a thoirt leis sa bhaga aige.
When Pompon and his parents prepare to go on a trip, Pompon must come to a decision as to what is essential for him to take in his bag. Pompon - Lana Beaton Rita/Tia - Mischa Macpherson Seòras - Calum MacKinnon Siùsaidh - Rebecca MacLennan Executive Producer - Bill Macleòid Producer - May Smart Producer - Mairi Macleod Editor - Phil Reed.

programme.desc:
Tha cuid dhe na rudan as fheàrr le Àtaidh agus Tilidh a dhìth. A bheil cuideigin air an goid? ’S e rùn-dìomhair a th’ ann!
Some of Abney and Teal’s favourite objects are missing. Has there been a robbery? It’s a mystery! Teal - Linda MacLeod Abney - Tony Kearney Producer - Linda MacLeod Executive Producer - Bill Macleòid Editor - Chas Chalmers Production Company - Solus Productions.

programme.title: Sionnach agus Maigheach (Fox & Hare)
programme.desc:
Tha Sionnach airson ’s gum bi co-là-breith sònraichte aig Maigheach. Tha cuireadh aig Comhachag is Tosg, fhad ’s a bheir iad prèasant brèagha thuice, leithid dìthean le fàileadh cùbhraidh. Chan eil sin cho furasta ’s a shaoileas iad. Fhad ’s a tha iad trang a’ lorg nam prèasantan tha Maigheach air bhioran ’s I a’ feitheamh gus an tòisich am pàrtaidh co-là-breith aice.
Fox wants to give Hare the best birthday ever. Owl and Tusk are invited, but only if they bring a nice present, like a beautifully scented flower. But that is not quite as easy as it seems. All the while Hare is kept waiting for her birthday party to start. Director - Linda MacLeod Production Company - Solus Productions.
